newsitem.title: GERMANY: Would-be "German Blair" says Kohl hard to beat.
newsitem.headline: Would-be "German Blair" says Kohl hard to beat.

text.p: The opposition politician who hopes to be "Germany's Tony Blair" warned on Monday that Chancellor Helmut Kohl would be a far tougher opponent to unseat next year than Britain's John Major proved to be last week.

Gerhard Schroeder, the pro-business Social Democrat hoping to gain most from the fresh breeze Blair's victory brought to the European left, said his SPD must fast adopt more modern stands on economic and technology policy if it wanted to win.
"We have to remember that Helmut Kohl is not John Major," he added in an interview with the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung.
"Helmut Kohl is a far more dangerous opponent that John Major was for the Labour party in the final phase of his government," the Lower Saxony state premier said.
Blair's landslide election victory has set the Social Democrats on a frenzied search for parallels they hope will help them return to power in October 1998 after 16 years in opposition.

Apart from some feeling it might be time for a change, though, the comparisons tend to highlight the differences between Britain and Germany, especially how much today's SPD resembles the pre-Blair Labour party rather than New Labour.

Unlike Major's Tories, Kohl's Christian Democrats are almost all solidly behind the chancellor's bid for re-election. There is no comparison between his few internal critics and the hostile factions that almost tore the Conservative party apart.
Schroeder, 53, has stressed in several recent interviews that Germany had to take the initiative in new technologies to help create jobs to fight record unemployment.
"With new technologies, be it information or biotechnology, we have got used to discussing the risks first and overlooking the opportunities," he said. "We have to change this."
But one Blair tactic Schroeder does not want to copy is the way the British leader took charge long before the election.
The SPD plans to name its challenger to Kohl only in April 1998, a month after the Lower Saxony state election Schroeder has to win if he is to have a fighting chance against Kohl.
But the Blair effect also means pressure to choose soon between Schroeder and SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine.
Heide Simonis, SPD premier of Schleswig-Holstein state and dark horse pick to someday be Germany's first woman chancellor candidate, called at the weekend for a quick decision.
But naming a candidate means choosing a platform, because the two men represent clearly different policies.

Schroeder, who is more popular outside the SPD than inside it, stands for pragmatic pro-business reforms while Lafontaine stands closer to the trade unions, left-wingers and interest groups that have dominated the party since the early 1980s.
Lafontaine, the SPD's failed 1990 standard bearer, has sought to win voter sympathy with strong opposition to Kohl.
But, as the Allgemeine Zeitung in Mainz wrote in an editorial: "The voters rewarded Blair for his position, not his opposition."

Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung also saw Blair's victory as a problem for the SPD. "New Labour's success will lead the German Social Democrats astray, back to their familiar old mistakes like in-fighting at the top."
Schroeder's relations with the Greens, the SPD's probable coalition partner if the two were to poll more than Kohl's centre-right government, also carry the potential for problems.
Schroeder had a coalition with the Greens in his state in the early 1990s but threw them out as soon as he won a one-seat majority at the last state election in 1994.
The SPD and Greens now lead Kohl's coalition in opinion polls by 47 to 44 percent, according to the latest Emnid poll.
